## Overview

A rotation describes an orientation or an orientation change. It does not, by itself, describe the path taken, the location of a joint, the forces that produced the motion, or the energy transferred. These distinctions matter when comparing pelvis and thorax motion, interpreting a clubface angle, or building a humanoid model.

This reference and the [interactive converter](rotation-converter.html) use **right-handed active rotations of column vectors**. For a vector rotated within one coordinate system, $v'=Rv$. For coordinates of the same physical vector in different frames, $v^A=R_{AB}v^B$: the columns of $R_{AB}$ are the axes of frame $B$ expressed in $A$. These interpretations share the same algebra; declare which one a measurement or calculation uses. All mathematical angles below are in radians. Quaternions use Hamilton multiplication and scalar-first order $(w,x,y,z)$.

| Representation | Numbers Stored | Constraints and Ambiguities |
|---|---|---|
| $R\in SO(3)$ | 9 | $R^TR=I$, $\det R=1$; three independent degrees of freedom |
| Unit quaternion $q\in S^3$ | 4 | Unit norm; $q$ and $-q$ give the same orientation |
| Euler angles | 3 | Axis order and moving/fixed-axis convention are essential; singular coordinate charts |
| Axis-angle $(n,\theta)$ | 4 | Unit axis; identity axis undefined; equivalent angle/axis choices |
| Rotation vector $\rho=\theta n\in\mathbb R^3$ | 3 | $[\rho]_\times\in\mathfrak{so}(3)$; logarithm branches and a half-turn ambiguity |

The number of stored scalars is not the number of physical degrees of freedom. A unit quaternion avoids Euler gimbal lock, but choosing a unique quaternion from every orientation cannot also give a globally continuous choice.

## Rotation Matrices

The special orthogonal group is

$$SO(3)=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^TR=I,\ \det R=1\}.$$

Orthogonality alone also admits reflections with determinant $-1$. A reflection is not a rotation. Composition follows frame cancellation:

$$v^A=R_{AB}(R_{BC}v^C),\qquad R_{AC}=R_{AB}R_{BC},\qquad R_{BA}=R_{AB}^T.$$

The rightmost transformation acts first. In a single frame, $R_z(\pi/2)R_x(\pi/2)e_y=e_z$, whereas reversing the factors gives $R_x(\pi/2)R_z(\pi/2)e_y=-e_x$. The two valid compositions describe different motions.

### Standard Rotation Matrices

$$R_x(\alpha)=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\0&\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha\end{bmatrix},$$

$$R_y(\beta)=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\beta&0&\sin\beta\\0&1&0\\-\sin\beta&0&\cos\beta\end{bmatrix},$$

$$R_z(\gamma)=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\gamma&-\sin\gamma&0\\\sin\gamma&\cos\gamma&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}.$$

For any $a,b$, $[a]_\times b=a\times b$, where

$$[a]_\times=\begin{bmatrix}0&-a_z&a_y\\a_z&0&-a_x\\-a_y&a_x&0\end{bmatrix}.$$

## Euler Angles

**Intrinsic ZYX** means yaw about the initial $z$ axis, pitch about the resulting $y$ axis, then roll about the resulting $x$ axis:

$$R=R_z(\psi)R_y(\theta)R_x(\phi).$$

It is equivalent to fixed-axis XYZ rotations applied in the temporal order roll, pitch, yaw. Calling either sequence merely “ZYX” without saying which axes move is incomplete. Here $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$ always means yaw, pitch, roll in that matrix product.

### Converting Euler Angles to Rotation Matrix

With $c_a=\cos a$ and $s_a=\sin a$,

$$R=\begin{bmatrix}
c_\psi c_\theta&c_\psi s_\theta s_\phi-s_\psi c_\phi&c_\psi s_\theta c_\phi+s_\psi s_\phi\\
s_\psi c_\theta&s_\psi s_\theta s_\phi+c_\psi c_\phi&s_\psi s_\theta c_\phi-c_\psi s_\phi\\
-s_\theta&c_\theta s_\phi&c_\theta c_\phi
\end{bmatrix}.$$

On the principal chart $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$,

$$\psi=\operatorname{atan2}(R_{21},R_{11}),\qquad
\phi=\operatorname{atan2}(R_{32},R_{33}),$$

$$\theta=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-R_{31},\sqrt{R_{11}^2+R_{21}^2}\right).$$

The familiar $-\arcsin(R_{31})$ is algebraically equivalent on this chart for an exact rotation. The atan2 form retains information in the small cosine terms when $R_{31}$ rounds to $\pm1$.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Gimbal Lock

At ZYX pitch $+\pi/2$, orientation determines $\psi-\phi$; at $-\pi/2$, it determines $\psi+\phi$. Choose $\phi=0$ and $\psi=\operatorname{atan2}(-R_{12},R_{22})$ at either lock. The rigid body retains its physical rotational freedom; the three-angle chart loses local independence.

The condition depends on the convention. Proper Euler ZYZ, $R_z(\alpha)R_y(\beta)R_z(\gamma)$, locks at $\beta=0$ or $\pi$, not at $\pi/2$. Near a chart singularity, coordinate uncertainty can be large even when orientation uncertainty is small. Changing representation does not remove sensor noise.
:::

### Euler Rates and Angular Velocity

Differentiating the declared product gives spatial angular velocity

$$\omega_s=\begin{bmatrix}
0&-\sin\psi&\cos\psi\cos\theta\\
0&\cos\psi&\sin\psi\cos\theta\\
1&0&-\sin\theta
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\dot\psi\\\dot\theta\\\dot\phi\end{bmatrix}.$$

The columns are the successive rotation axes expressed in the same frame. Their determinant magnitude is $|\cos\theta|$. At yaw $\pi/2$, pitch zero and only $\dot\phi=1$ rad/s, $\omega_s=(0,1,0)$ rad/s: a roll-coordinate rate is not automatically the world $x$ component. Peak Euler-coordinate rates from different conventions therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable segment-speed measurements.

## Axis-Angle Representation

For a unit axis $n$ and angle $\theta$,

$$R=I+\sin\theta[n]_\times+(1-\cos\theta)[n]_\times^2
=\exp(\theta[n]_\times).$$

This is Rodrigues' formula. The identity $1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ is useful for small angles. Any nonzero input axis can first be normalized; a zero axis cannot define a nonzero rotation.

A principal representation uses $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$. For $0<\theta<\pi$ the directed axis is determined. At identity any axis gives the same zero rotation; at a half-turn both $n$ and $-n$ give the same rotation. Outside the principal range, equivalent descriptions include $(n,\theta+2k\pi)$ and $(-n,-\theta)$.

A matrix fixes the direction of this equivalent rotation axis, not its location in physical space. Rotating a club about different parallel lines produces the same orientation change and different translations. A full rigid-body displacement needs position as well as orientation; see the [screw-theory reference](screw-theory-reference.html).

## Exponential Coordinates (Lie Algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$)

The **rotation vector** $\rho=\theta n$ has three real components; its skew matrix belongs to the Lie algebra:

$$\rho\in\mathbb R^3,\qquad [\rho]_\times\in\mathfrak{so}(3),\qquad R=\exp([\rho]_\times).$$

Where a selected logarithm branch is defined, $[\rho]_\times=\log R$ and $\rho=(\log R)^\vee$, with vee the inverse of the skew map. A vector is not literally a $3\times3$ matrix logarithm. The principal vector cannot describe accumulated revolutions: 0 and $2\pi n$ exponentiate to the same orientation.

For a differentiable orientation history,

$$[\omega_s]_\times=\dot R R^T,\qquad [\omega_b]_\times=R^T\dot R,\qquad \omega_s=R\omega_b.$$

Angular velocity has units rad/s; a rotation vector uses radians. In a smooth rotation-vector chart,

$$\omega_s=J_l(\rho)\dot\rho,\qquad \omega_b=J_l(-\rho)\dot\rho,$$

$$J_l(\rho)=I+\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta^2}[\rho]_\times+
\frac{\theta-\sin\theta}{\theta^3}[\rho]_\times^2,\qquad \theta=\|\rho\|.$$

At zero use coefficient limits $1/2$ and $1/6$. For fixed-axis motion $\rho=\theta(t)n$, the cross terms annihilate $\dot\rho$, giving $\omega=\dot\theta n$. For a changing axis, simply differentiating rotation-vector components generally gives the wrong angular velocity. Crossing a principal-logarithm branch requires a continuity strategy; exponential coordinates do not provide a global singularity-free three-parameter chart.

## Quaternions

A unit Hamilton quaternion is

$$q=(w,v)=\left(\cos\frac\theta2,\ n\sin\frac\theta2\right),\qquad w^2+v^Tv=1.$$

### Quaternion to Rotation Matrix

$$R=\begin{bmatrix}
1-2(y^2+z^2)&2(xy-wz)&2(xz+wy)\\
2(xy+wz)&1-2(x^2+z^2)&2(yz-wx)\\
2(xz-wy)&2(yz+wx)&1-2(x^2+y^2)
\end{bmatrix}.$$

Normalize a finite nonzero quaternion first. Rescaling by its largest component before taking the norm prevents avoidable floating-point overflow or underflow.

### Quaternion Composition

For $p=(p_w,p_v)$ and $q=(q_w,q_v)$,

$$p\otimes q=(p_wq_w-p_v^Tq_v,\ p_wq_v+q_wp_v+p_v\times q_v).$$

Then $R(p\otimes q)=R(p)R(q)$, so $q$ acts first. For unit $q$, the conjugate $(w,-v)$ represents the inverse. Scalar-last libraries require reordering; changing component order does not change the declared multiplication convention automatically.

### Quaternion Derivative

For body-to-world orientation, the Hamilton convention gives

$$\dot q=\tfrac12(0,\omega_s)\otimes q
=\tfrac12 q\otimes(0,\omega_b).$$

Both velocities describe the same physical rotation in different frames. Mixing one velocity's components with the other's multiplication side changes the motion.

::: {.callout-note}
## Double Cover

$q$ and $-q$ describe one orientation. For nearby sampled orientations, negating a sample when its dot product with the previous one is negative selects a locally continuous, shorter quaternion arc. This assumes the physical increment is resolved by the sampling. At a zero dot product the shortest rotation is not unique. Sparse samples do not reveal extra revolutions or the actual path; a shortest-path interpolation is a modeling choice. An integrated continuous quaternion history need not be forced into the half-sphere $w\geq0$ at every step.
:::

## Conversion Summary Table

| Conversion | Stable Procedure and Limits |
|---|---|
| Axis-angle → $R$ | Normalize a nonzero axis; apply Rodrigues or its equivalent half-angle formula |
| Quaternion → $R$ | Normalize a nonzero quaternion; use the unit formula above |
| $R$ → quaternion | Validate $SO(3)$; recover the largest quaternion component first, then normalize |
| $R$ → axis-angle | From a quaternion with $w\geq0$, use $\theta=2\operatorname{atan2}(\|v\|,w)$; $n=v/\|v\|$ unless identity |
| $R$ → ZYX | Use atan2 pitch and the declared generic or gimbal-lock branch |
| Rotation vector → $R$ | Identity at zero; otherwise normalize its direction and use its norm as angle |

### Why the Largest Quaternion Component Matters

For an exact rotation,

$$\begin{bmatrix}w^2\\x^2\\y^2\\z^2\end{bmatrix}
=\frac14\begin{bmatrix}1+\operatorname{tr}R\\1+2R_{11}-\operatorname{tr}R\\1+2R_{22}-\operatorname{tr}R\\1+2R_{33}-\operatorname{tr}R\end{bmatrix}.$$

The four squares sum to one, so the largest component has magnitude at least $1/2$. Choose it positive and recover the other components from identities such as

$$4wx=R_{32}-R_{23},\quad4wy=R_{13}-R_{31},\quad4wz=R_{21}-R_{12},$$

$$4xy=R_{12}+R_{21},\quad4xz=R_{13}+R_{31},\quad4yz=R_{23}+R_{32}.$$

Divide only by four times the selected component, then normalize. The denominator is at least two for an exact rotation. Always dividing by $4w$ fails near a half-turn. The trace-based angle $\arccos((\operatorname{tr}R-1)/2)$ and axis formula using $1/(2\sin\theta)$ are useful derivations, but lose numerical information near zero or $\pi$; they are not unconditional algorithms.

## Python Implementation

Run this example from the AffineDrift repository root with its Python dependencies installed. The small reference adapter reuses the [reviewed Volume 0 quaternion implementation](The_Geometry_of_Motion/quarto/vol0_ch04_rotations_se3.html). The complete implementation and tests are in `src/tools/rotation_reference_examples.py` and `tests/test_rotation_representations_reference.py`.

The Python matrix tolerance is $10^{-10}$. The browser accepts maximum entry orthogonality and determinant residuals below $10^{-5}$ to accommodate rounded editable matrices. Those residuals are not confidence intervals. Approximate accepted matrices and normalized output representations may differ by rounding; neither adapter promises a statistically justified or nearest-rotation fit. The numerical lock threshold is $|\cos\theta|<10^{-12}$.

```python
import numpy as np

from src.tools.rotation_reference_examples import (
    axis_angle_to_rotation as axis_angle_to_R,
    euler_zyx_to_rotation as euler_zyx_to_R,
    quaternion_to_rotation as quaternion_to_R,
    rotation_to_axis_angle as R_to_axis_angle,
    rotation_to_euler_zyx as R_to_euler_zyx,
    rotation_to_quaternion as R_to_quaternion,
)

# --- Verification: compare reconstructed orientations, not ambiguous coordinates.
axis = np.array([-1.0, 2.0, -3.0]) / np.sqrt(14)
for angle in [1e-12, 0.7, np.pi - 1e-8, np.pi, np.pi + 1e-8]:
    original = axis_angle_to_R(axis, angle)
    recovered_axis, recovered_angle = R_to_axis_angle(original)
    recovered_q = R_to_quaternion(original)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        axis_angle_to_R(recovered_axis, recovered_angle), original, atol=2e-14
    )
    np.testing.assert_allclose(quaternion_to_R(recovered_q), original, atol=2e-14)

for pitch in [np.pi / 2, -np.pi / 2, np.pi / 2 - 1e-8]:
    original = euler_zyx_to_R(0.7, pitch, -0.9)
    angles = R_to_euler_zyx(original)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(euler_zyx_to_R(*angles), original, atol=2e-14)
```

## From Orientation to Golf Mechanics

For calibrated segment-to-world matrices $R_{WA}$ and $R_{WB}$, relative segment orientation is

$$R_{AB}=R_{WA}^TR_{WB}.$$

This is more precise than subtracting independently extracted yaw angles. With both segment angular velocities expressed in world coordinates,

$$\omega_{B/A}^{B}=R_{WB}^T(\omega_B^W-\omega_A^W).$$

Anatomical axis calibration, measurement times, filtering and Euler convention must be declared before a relative angle is called pelvic rotation, thorax rotation or a joint excursion. A common fixed world-frame rotation cancels from $R_{AB}$; independent segment-calibration errors do not.

For a clubface normal fixed in the club frame, $n_W=R_{WC}n_C$ and

$$\dot n_W=\omega_C^W\times n_W.$$

Angular velocity parallel to the normal does not change that normal instantaneously. Thus an orientation component, angular-speed magnitude and the rate of change of a delivery direction answer different questions. A face normal alone also leaves rotation about that normal undetermined.

For small spatial orientation error $\delta\vartheta$,

$$R_{\mathrm{measured}}\approx\exp([\delta\vartheta]_\times)R_{\mathrm{true}},\qquad
\delta n\approx-[n]_\times\delta\vartheta.$$

Its normal covariance is approximately $[n]_\times\Sigma_\vartheta[n]_\times^T$ in that same frame. Shared calibration and synchronization errors create correlations; treating each segment's uncertainty as independent can misstate relative-motion uncertainty. Differencing successive orientations requires a declared time interval and a local logarithm branch, and amplifies noise as the interval shrinks. An isolated orientation cannot determine angular velocity.

Finally, rotational kinetic energy needs physical central inertia and angular velocity in a common basis:

$$K=\tfrac12m\|v_C\|^2+\tfrac12\omega^TI_C\omega.$$

Moment power is $\tau\cdot\omega$, with force power at its actual application point added where appropriate. Neither a large rotation angle nor a peak Euler rate demonstrates proximal-to-distal energy transfer. Those arguments require the [segment and interface work ledger](The_Physics_of_Golf/quarto/ch10_energy_transfer.html), contact constraints, continuing actuator work and uncertainty. Representation changes preserve the physical problem when every vector, inertia and derivative is transformed consistently.

## Sources and Scope

Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, *Modern Robotics* (2017), provide the rotation, frame and exponential framework. The official [rotation-exponential transcript](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/3-2-3-exponential-coordinates-of-rotation-part-2-of-2/) explains the constant-axis construction; the [angular-velocity transcript](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/3-2-2-angular-velocities/) distinguishes body and spatial representations. The numerical branches and verification examples here are specified explicitly rather than attributed wholesale to those transcripts.

SciPy's [Euler conversion documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation.as_euler.html) explains intrinsic/extrinsic sequences and its singularity convention. Its [matrix conversion documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation.from_matrix.html) describes fitting an approximate rotation; that behavior must not be mistaken for the stricter input validation used here. These mathematical and software sources do not validate a golfer-specific anatomical calibration, coaching intervention or energy-transfer claim.
